opus-5.5.text:
Well, I love that example because it shows that the choice isn't between "no regulation" and "ban everything." There's a middle path that's actually worked for decades.

If you want to build a nuclear reactor, the regulator doesn't sit there and tell you how to design it. They don't say, "You must use this particular cooling system or this particular fuel rod geometry." Instead, they set a quantitative safety requirement. Roughly speaking, you have to show that the probability of a core meltdown is below something like one in ten thousand per reactor-year. Then the burden of proof is on the company. You come in with your engineering analysis, your fault trees, your probabilistic risk assessment, and you convince the experts that you meet the bar.

That's beautiful for a couple of reasons. First, it's technology-neutral. It doesn't lock in today's designs, so if you invent a cleverer, safer reactor, great, you can bring it to market. The innovation goes into figuring out how to be safe, not into lobbying. Second, it puts the responsibility where it belongs. It's not the public's job to prove your product is dangerous. It's your job to prove it's safe enough.

And honestly, this is how we treat basically every other powerful technology. Drugs have clinical trials. Airplanes have certification. Nobody says the FDA has killed the biotech industry. It's the reason people trust medicine enough to take it.

So when people in AI say any regulation will stifle innovation, I point to nuclear and say, look, you can have clear, measurable safety standards and still let companies compete like crazy to meet them. For AI, that might mean: before you deploy a system above a certain capability level, you have to demonstrate, quantitatively, that the risk of it helping someone make a bioweapon or escaping human control is below some threshold. If you can't show that, you don't ship yet. Just like you wouldn't switch on a reactor where you had no idea what the meltdown probability was.

The irony is that right now AI is less regulated than sandwich shops. We'd never accept that for nuclear power, and I think we shouldn't accept it for a technology that many of its own builders say could be even more powerful.

r001.rationale: It says a company must demonstrate that the probability of core meltdown is below roughly one per 10,000 reactor-years to meet the regulator’s safety requirement.

r002.rationale: It describes the standard as technology-neutral: regulators do not prescribe a design, so companies can bring forward different designs that meet the safety bar.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a wonderful example because it shows that safety and innovation aren't enemies. When we build a nuclear reactor, we don't just hope it's safe or ask the company to pinky-promise that it's safe. The regulator says: you have to demonstrate, quantitatively, that the probability of a core meltdown is below some number, something like one in ten thousand per reactor-year, or whatever the specific threshold is. And crucially, the burden of proof is on the company, not on the government or the public.

What I love about this is that the regulator doesn't tell the engineers how to build the reactor. It doesn't say you have to use this coolant or that containment design. It just sets the bar and says: show us. That unleashes enormous creativity, because engineers are free to come up with any design they want, as long as they can prove it meets the standard. You get passive safety systems, new fuel types, all kinds of clever ideas, precisely because the incentive is to meet a clear, measurable target rather than to lobby your way around a vague rule.

And compare that to what we have in AI right now, which is basically nothing. A sandwich shop in Boston has to meet stricter safety requirements than a company releasing a model that can help someone synthesize a bioweapon. If you tried to launch a reactor with the attitude of "we're not sure if it'll melt down, but let's ship it and see," you'd be laughed out of the room, or arrested.

So the lesson I draw is: pick the risks you actually care about, make them quantitative, put the burden of proof on the developer, and then get out of the way. The companies that are good at safety will thrive, the ones that aren't will adapt, and we'll get both the innovation and the protection. We've done it with airplanes, with drugs, with nuclear power. There's no reason we can't do it with AI, except that we haven't yet decided to.

r002.rationale: It says the regulator does not dictate how to build the reactor and engineers may use any design if they prove it meets the quantitative safety standard.

astra-6.text:
Because you can set a quantitative safety requirement without prescribing exactly how the reactor has to be built. You can say, for example, that the probability of a catastrophic release of radioactivity has to be below some very small threshold, and then put the burden on the company to demonstrate that its design meets that requirement before it operates.

That leaves room for innovation. If somebody comes up with a completely different reactor design that’s safer and cheaper, great! They don’t have to copy the old design; they have to meet the safety standard. And the requirement actually creates an incentive to innovate on safety.

I think that’s a useful principle for AI, too. The government doesn’t need to dictate the architecture or how you train your system. But if you’re building something that could cause catastrophic harm, you should have to demonstrate that the risk is acceptably low before deploying it. Of course, figuring out how to measure and demonstrate that for AI is a major challenge. But that’s the challenge we should be working on.

r001.rationale: The response gives no one-in-10,000-years threshold and does not say reactor builders must demonstrate that meltdown risk is below it before construction. It mentions a small threshold for catastrophic radioactive release before operation.

r002.rationale: The response says a company with a different reactor design need not copy the old design; it must meet the safety standard.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, because we don’t just tell someone building a nuclear reactor, “Please make it safe.” We require them to demonstrate, before they turn it on, that the probability of certain catastrophic failures is below a specified threshold. And then engineers can innovate on how to meet those requirements. You’re specifying the safety outcome, rather than prescribing every detail of the design.

I think that’s a useful model for AI. Instead of arguing about whether regulation is pro-innovation or anti-innovation, we should ask: what risks are acceptable, and what evidence should a company provide before exposing everyone else to those risks? If you can meet the safety standard with a clever new approach, great. That’s innovation we should welcome.

r001.rationale: The response mentions demonstrating that catastrophic failure probabilities fall below a specified threshold, but gives no threshold of one in 10,000 years.

r002.rationale: It says engineers can innovate in how they meet the safety requirements and that regulation specifies the safety outcome rather than every design detail.
